title: Unique IDs at Scale
summary: Giving every row a name nobody else will ever use — without one counter everyone has to queue for.

goals.text: Why database counters break under sharding
UUIDs — and what random keys do to an index
Time-ordered ids: UUID v7 and Snowflake
Clocks that step back, and what ids leak

steps.title: Every row needs a name
body: Orders, users, payments: every row needs an identifier that is unique — for ever. Other tables point at it, URLs contain it, support staff read it out over the phone.
With one database this is free. An AUTO_INCREMENT (or SERIAL) column hands out 1001, 1002, 1003… and the database guarantees no number is ever used twice.

callout.text: A counter gives you more than uniqueness: the ids are small, and sorting by id sorts by creation time. Watch which of those gifts each alternative keeps.

steps.title: Two shards, two counters
body: The orders table gets sharded (see Sharding). Each shard is its own database with its own counter — and both of them have just handed out 1004.
Two different orders now share an id. A link to /orders/1004, a cache entry, a refund: each could mean either one. And the day you merge or re-split shards, the rows collide.

callout.text: Uniqueness has to hold across the whole system, not just inside one machine.

changes: + Shard B, with its own counter

steps.title: Way 1 — one counter for everyone
body: Move the counter out of the shards into a small service whose only job is to hand out the next number: a ticket server. Before each insert, an app server asks it for an id.
Uniqueness is back, and ids still sort by time. But every insert now costs an extra round trip — and if the ticket server is down, nobody can create anything.

callout.text: Flickr ran two ticket servers for years — one handing out odd numbers, the other even — so that either could fail without stopping the site.

changes: ~ Every insert asks it for an id first
− A new single point of failure

steps.title: Hand out blocks, not single numbers
body: Ask less often. Each app server reserves a whole block — say 1,000 ids — in one call and hands them out from memory. That’s one round trip per thousand inserts, and the app keeps working for a while if the ticket server is down.
The price: ids no longer follow creation time across servers (Server 2’s 2001 may be older than Server 1’s 1500), and a server that crashes takes the rest of its block with it, leaving gaps.

callout.text: Gaps are harmless. Never promise that ids are gap-free or strictly ordered — invoice numbers that legally must be gapless are a separate, deliberate counter.

steps.title: Way 2 — pick a number nobody else will
body: Or drop the coordination altogether. A UUID (version 4) is 122 random bits. Any server, phone or script can make one, with nobody to ask.
Can two collide? In principle. In practice you would have to generate a billion every second for about 86 years to reach a 50% chance of a single repeat.

callout.text: The cost is size: 128 bits, twice a normal id — and that id is copied into every index and every table that points at the row.

steps.title: Case: random ids and the index
body: The primary key lives in a B-tree, sorted by id (see Indexes). Counter ids always land on the last page, which stays in memory. Random ids land on a random page, every time.

Once the index is bigger than memory, most inserts must first fetch a cold page from disk, and pages split all over the tree. Insert throughput can drop several-fold, and the index ends up bloated with half-empty pages.

callout.text: It bites hardest where the table itself is stored in primary-key order — MySQL’s InnoDB, SQL Server — but every B-tree feels it.

changes: + Inside one shard: the primary-key index

card.title: Where does the next row go?
lines: counter id   → always the last page
! random id  → any page, every time

steps.title: Put the time in front
body: Keep the randomness, but lead with a timestamp. UUID v7 — and its cousin, ULID — starts with 48 bits of milliseconds, followed by random bits.
New ids are always larger than old ones, so inserts return to the right-hand edge of the index. They still need no coordination, and “sort by id” means “sort by creation time” again.

callout.text: If you want UUIDs as primary keys, use version 7. Keep version 4 for tokens that must be impossible to guess.

changes: ~ Inserts append to the last page again

steps.title: Way 3 — Snowflake ids
body: Twitter needed ids that fit in 64 bits, sort by time, and could be minted tens of thousands of times a second with no central counter. Its answer, Snowflake, packs three fields into one number.

A millisecond timestamp, the machine id of the generator, and a sequence that counts up within the millisecond. Two machines can never collide, because their machine ids differ; one machine never repeats, because of the sequence.

callout.text: Each machine can mint 4,096 ids per millisecond. Discord, Instagram and many others use the same idea with slightly different bit splits.

changes: + Every server gets a machine id at startup

steps.title: Case: the clock steps back
body: Snowflake ids are unique only if a machine’s clock never repeats a millisecond. But clocks get corrected: time sync notices Server 1 is two seconds fast and sets it back. For two seconds it would stamp ids with times it has already used — duplicates.
The guard is simple. Remember the last timestamp you issued; if the clock now reads earlier, wait (or refuse to issue ids) until time has caught up.

callout.text: The other way to break it: two machines with the same machine id. Assign them from one place — a config service, or bits of something already unique — never by hand.

changes: + Generator waits until the clock passes its last stamp
~ No duplicates — that server pauses inserts for 2 s

steps.title: Case: what an id gives away
body: Ids end up in URLs, and people read them. A competitor places an order on Monday (#1004) and another on Tuesday (#1250) — and now knows you take about 246 orders a day.
Sequential ids are also easy to walk: change /invoices/1004 to /invoices/1005 and see what comes back. Time-based ids reveal exactly when each thing was created.

callout.text: Two defences, and you need the second one regardless: show a separate random public id, and check authorization on every request (see Authorization). An unguessable id is not access control.

changes: + A competitor reading ids out of URLs
~ Public ids → random; internal keys stay ordered

steps.title: Which id for which job
body:
SizeTime-sortedNeeds
DB counter64 bitsYesOne database
Ticket blocks64 bitsRoughlyA ticket service
UUID v4128 bitsNoNothing
UUID v7128 bitsYesA clock
Snowflake64 bitsYesMachine ids + clock
One database? Use its counter. Many writers and nothing shared? UUID v7. Compact numeric ids at very high volume? Snowflake.

callout.text: There is no best id — only the properties your system needs: size, ordering, independence and secrecy.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A per-database counter stops being unique the moment you shard.
  • A ticket server restores it; handing out blocks removes the round trip per insert.
  • UUID v4 needs nobody, but scatters inserts across the index; UUID v7 puts time first to fix that.
  • Snowflake: time + machine id + sequence in 64 bits — guard against clocks stepping back.
  • Ids leak volume and timing. Never treat them as access control.
